title: Testing and Hardening a Tool
summary: A tool that crashes, hangs or shows wrong numbers is worse than none: people stop trusting it. This lesson hardens the chapter's tools: treating everything read from another process as untrusted input, validating snapshots, timeouts and reconnection, running with least privilege, and testing the logic separately from the platform code, including deliberately feeding it garbage.
markdown:
## Everything from outside is untrusted The telemetry block, pipe messages and memory read from another process all come from a different program, which may be an older or newer version, half-initialised, crashed in the middle of writing, or simply buggy. Treat it exactly like a file from the internet: | Check | Why | |---|---| | Header: magic, version, size (lesson 12.06) | Is this even the right kind of data? | | Sizes and counts against limits | A count of 2 billion monsters means corruption, not a busy floor | | Ranges | Health between 0 and its maximum; positions inside the map; frame time positive and below, say, 10 seconds | | Consistency | Frame number never goes backwards (except after a restart, which the process id change reveals) | | Strings | Fixed-size character arrays must contain a terminator within their size (lesson 2.08) | A value that fails a check is shown as invalid, not used to index arrays or size allocations. The practice task writes a validator returning a list of problems. ## Never hang Every wait in a tool needs a limit: - Sequence-lock reads retry a bounded number of times (lesson 12.04). - Pipe reads use overlapped I/O or a timeout, so a game that stops responding does not freeze the tool. - Opening the game's mapping happens on a timer, not in a tight loop. If the game is frozen, the tool should say so (lesson 12.05's "stale" state) and stay responsive. ## Least privilege The chapter's tools need very little: - Read-only views of the shared memory (`FILE_MAP_READ`). - `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION | SYNCHRONIZE` on the game's process, to watch whether it runs. - No administrator rights, ever: if a tool seems to need elevation, something in its design is wrong (lesson 6.08). Asking for little keeps the tool working for ordinary users and limits the harm any bug in it can do. ## Testing the logic Every practice task in this course has followed one structure: the logic (formatting, validation, version checks, statistics, protocols) is plain C++ with no Windows calls, tested in isolation; a thin platform layer does the Windows calls. That pays off most in tools: ```mermaid flowchart LR P["Platform layer
OpenFileMapping, ReadProcessMemory,
console output"] --> L["Logic
validate, decode, compute,
format: pure functions"] T["Unit tests
(chapter 17)"] --> L ``` - **Unit tests** feed the logic known inputs, including recorded real snapshots, and check the outputs. - **Garbage tests** feed it random bytes, truncated blocks, wrong versions, extreme values. The tool must report problems, never crash. Chapter 17 automates this as **fuzzing**. - **End-to-end tests** run the real game with a scripted input and check the tool shows what was expected. ## Failure modes to rehearse Before calling a tool done, try each of these on purpose: 1. Start the tool with no game running. 2. Start the game, then the tool; close the game; start it again. 3. Pause the game in the debugger while the tool watches. 4. Run two copies of the game. 5. Run an older and a newer build of the game against the same tool. 6. Corrupt the shared block from a test program (write random bytes into it). A tool that handles all six calmly can be trusted. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Using an untrusted count to size an allocation > A corrupt count of billions turns into a crash or an out-of-memory. Validate against a sensible limit first. > [!warning] Waiting without a timeout > A frozen game must not freeze its tools. > [!warning] Testing only the happy path > Rehearse the failure modes; they are what users will hit. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Why treat data from another process as untrusted? - Because other processes may be run by hackers - Because Windows changes the data when copying it between processes + It may be another version, half written or corrupt - Because shared memory is slower than normal memory > A count of 3 billion monsters is more likely a bug or a layout mismatch than a real number. ? Which waits in a tool need limits? + All of them, including retries and pipe reads - Only connection attempts - Only pipe reads - None, if the game is well written > A tool that hangs because the game froze is no help in finding why the game froze. ? What does "garbage testing" mean for a tool? - Running the tool on an old, slow computer - Deleting the tool's temporary files after each test - Testing the tool with no game running + Feeding its logic random and broken data to check it copes > Keeping the logic free of Windows calls is what makes it easy to feed it such data in tests. ? A telemetry snapshot says 3 billion monsters are alive. What should the tool do? + Reject the snapshot as invalid and report it - Display 3 billion - Allocate an array of 3 billion entries > Implausible values mean corruption or a version mismatch. ? Why keep a tool's logic free of Windows calls? - Windows calls are slow + So it can be unit-tested without a game - The compiler requires it > A thin platform layer around pure logic is easy to test. ? What rights does a read-only stats tool need on the game's process? - Full access - Administrator rights + Limited query information and synchronize > Least privilege: nothing more than its job needs. ```
ideas:
- Write a test program that maps Delve's telemetry for writing and fills it with random bytes once a second, and make sure the panel reports invalid data instead of crashing.
- Run through the six failure modes with your panel and fix whatever breaks.
- Put the panel's validation and formatting in a separate project with unit tests.
